missed.title: The ships' masts stand on nothing, a deck above the ship
missed.versions: all five, at 1920 and 1440, on both ships (clearest on the front ship; at Night the mast and its masthead light read as a lamp post standing in the town)
missed.observed: Each ship's mast runs up from deckTop, the top deck's roof, at mx = x1 - 0.3L. But the top deck (d=4) ends at b4 = x1 - 0.35L, and its sloped front ends at x1 - 0.311L. At mx the only structure is deck 3's top corner, one deck height (dh) lower. So the mast's foot hangs in the air about dh - 1 above the ship: 9 CSS px on the front ship at 1920 (L = 342, dh = 10.3), 7 on the back ship, and 7.6 on the front ship at 1440. In the Day render at 2x the front ship's mast is a thin line at x about 935 ending near y 710, with deck 3's corner at y 728 below it and the town showing between. At Night at 3x the masthead light on its pole reads as a street lamp among the houses.
missed.proposal: Stand each mast on the top deck, just back from its forward end, where a cruise ship's mast rises above the bridge. Moving the mast's x moves its masthead light and halo with it.
missed.why: 'Nothing floating' is one of the owner's recorded checks (DESIGN 19.5 step 4). This is the same kind of misalignment as today's fixes, and it is visible at the picture's real size as a pole that stops short of the ship.
missed.code: harbour() ship(), line 1397: change `const mx = x1 - L * 0.3` to `const mx = x1 - L * 0.38`. The top deck spans to x1 - 0.35L, so the foot at deckTop + 1 now lands on its roof, about 0.03L (10px at 1920) back from its forward corner. The halo and the isl-vnav-w light at line 1403 use mx and follow it. No r() is used, and the funnel (x0 + 0.2L to x0 + 0.285L) stays well clear. The mast is inside `one`, so its reflection follows too.
missed.truth_to_place: owner-st-johns-cruise-ship: the mast (with its radar and lights) rises from the top of the superstructure forward, above the bridge, not from open air ahead of it.

proposals.title: The far shore's lights are missing; only their columns are drawn
proposals.versions: Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night (the lights); Day (where the houses stand)
proposals.observed: Twelve columns of light run down the harbour from the far shore (x about 0.01 to 0.31), but the shore above them is a dark silhouette with no light points at all, at Dusk and Night. steps() builds shoreLights and uses them only for dayHouses and streakList columns. No s-vlight path is ever drawn for them. The header comment says 'the far shore's lights, each laying a broken column of light on the water'. Their y is also fixed at Y(0.582 + r()*0.014), while the shore's top falls from 0.575 to 0.602 toward its right end. By the numbers, points right of about 0.2W can stand up to about 5 CSS px above the land, and the Day houses share those points.
proposals.proposal: Draw the lights: a small s-vlight isl-vwin path (--i:0, stroke about 1.3) at the shoreLights points, as telescope() and wayIn() do. Place each point inside the shore's own silhouette, a share of the way down from its top at that x, so the lights and the Day houses sit on the land.
proposals.why: Every light should come as a set: the light, its halo and its column. At the moment the water carries reflections of lights that are not there, and the owner would notice the dark shore above lit columns.
proposals.code: steps(), lines 757-763. Add a topAt(x) that interpolates farShore[0..5] (already in px). In the loop at line 761, keep the same two r() calls so the rest of the piece's random stream is unchanged: const x = X(0.01 + r()*0.3), t = topAt(x); shoreLights.push([x, t + (Y(0.6) - t) * (0.25 + r()*0.5)]). After line 763 add: s += `<path class="s-vlight isl-vwin" style="--i:0" d="${lightsD(shoreLights)}" stroke-width="1.3"/>`. lightsD is the module-level helper at line 898, available at call time. s-vlight is already hidden by Day (layout-art.css line 155).

proposals.title: The turret's slit sits on the edge between its faces, and its shade spills into the sky
proposals.versions: all five (the translucent block shows most by Day, at 1920 and 1440)
proposals.observed: (a) The turret's lit slit is centred at gx1 - tw2/2, 3 px wide (758.8 to 761.8 CSS px at 1920). The shaded right face starts at gx1 - tw2*0.45 (761.4), so the slit straddles the edge where the lit face meets the shaded one, the same fault as Betty's Hope's doors. (b) The shade is one rectangle from lb up to lb - th - Y(0.02), the top of the merlons. It fills the crenels between them, and the turret's right corner has no merlon. Because isl-vpshade is --isl-near at 0.3 opacity, that part is a translucent teal block laid over the sky beside the last merlon, clearly visible by Day at the turret's top right.
proposals.proposal: Move the slit to the middle of the turret's lit face (centre gx1 - tw2*0.725). Space the three turret merlons from corner to corner, so a merlon stands on each corner as the main parapet has on its left. Shade only stone: the turret body from lb up to lb - th, plus the part of each merlon that lies right of the face's edge. The shaded face then turns the corner through the crenellation, as the Court House's side face now runs through its parapet and coping.
proposals.why: Two of the owner's own rules from today apply here. A door or window sits in the middle of a face, never on the edge between two faces (Betty's Hope). A side face carries all the way up (the Court House). The owner also rejects boxes over the sky.
proposals.code: steps(): the turret merlons at lines 789-792 become const mw = tw2/5; for i in 0..2: mx = gx1 - tw2 + i*(tw2 - mw)/2, width mw. For the shade at line 798: const sx = gx1 - tw2*0.45; let tsh = `M${F(sx)} ${F(lb)}V${F(lb - th)}H${F(gx1)}V${F(lb)}Z`; for each turret merlon, a = Math.max(mx, sx); if (mx + mw > a) tsh += rect(a, lb - th - Y(0.02), mx + mw - a, Y(0.02)). For the slit at line 809: lit += `M${F(gx1 - tw2*0.725 - 1.5)} ...` (the rest unchanged).

proposals.title: The century plant is in front of the stairs but behind the lantern standing on them
proposals.observed: The plant's rosette is at (0.66W, 0.66H), lower on the slope and so nearer the viewer. Its stalk is drawn after the stairs, so it passes in front of the treads. The plant is drawn before the lanterns, though. The second landing's lantern (about 0.649W) stands among the stalk's lower-left flower branches, which reach 0.642W, and its post and glass are painted over those branches. The plant is therefore in front of the stairs but behind a lantern that stands on those stairs.
proposals.proposal: Move the century plant right by about X(0.03), so its branches (then about 0.67 to 0.73W) clear the landing lantern and its halo. The stalk still crosses in front of the upper flight, which is the depth it should have. Drawing the plant after the lanterns would also fix the order, but it would lay the branches across the lantern's glass.
proposals.why: Draw order has to agree with depth, and at 3x the lantern post visibly cuts across the branches. This is the kind of small contradiction the owner catches.
proposals.code: steps(), line 836: const cpx = X(0.69) (was X(0.66)); sx2 and the branch loop at lines 842-847 follow cpx. The second landing lantern's x is x0 + 14*dx + 1.5*land, about X(0.649) (lanterns built at lines 818-828).

proposals.title: Give the yacht at anchor its reflection, and a furled mainsail on a boom
proposals.observed: The yacht has a hull, sheer line, mast and two stays, a riding light with its halo, and a column of light below it. It is the only hull in these pieces with no mirrored reflection (the telescope's boats and Sailing Week's fleet have one). With the mast and two symmetrical stays and no boom, the rig reads a little like an A-frame tent.
proposals.proposal: Mirror the hull and mast about the waterline (by), faint (opacity 0.15) and clipped to the sea, before the hull is drawn. Add a boom from the mast about Y(0.05) above the deck toward the stern, carrying a furled mainsail: one pale stroke, about 2 px, with a round cap. The boom also tells the viewer which end is the stern.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.3 calls for a reflection under every hull. A furled sail on its boom is what makes a boat read as a yacht at anchor rather than a triangle.
proposals.code: steps(), lines 765-770. Build const yacht = hull path + mast/stays path (the strings at lines 768 and 770). Before them: s += `<g clip-path="url(#islsea)" opacity=".15"><g transform="translate(0 ${F(2*by)}) scale(1 -1)">${yacht}</g></g>`. Boom: `<path class="isl-vsheer" d="M${F(bx)} ${F(by - Y(0.05))}L${F(bx - X(0.026))} ${F(by - Y(0.042))}" stroke-width="${F(Math.max(2, Y(0.008)))}" stroke-linecap="round"/>`. No r() calls are added.

proposals.title: Carry the stone courses up the turret and across the broken wall
proposals.observed: The courses (line 800) run from gx0 to gx1 and stop at lb - lh, the main parapet. The turret's upper part, above the parapet up to lb - th, is plain. The broken wall stepping down the slope to the left (gx0 - lw*0.32 to gx0) has no courses at all, so it reads as a flat pale block beside the coursed building behind the top lantern.
proposals.proposal: Run the same courses (spacing Y(0.022), same stroke) up the turret between gx1 - tw2 and gx1, as far as lb - th. Start each lower course at the broken wall's own left edge for that height (its three steps are at lh*0.3, 0.42 and 0.55), so the wall reads as the same masonry, ruined. Optionally continue the mid string course (line 802) across the turret to gx1.
proposals.why: This is the Court House lesson in small: the structure keeps going round the whole form instead of stopping at a line. The lookout is the steps' destination and deserves the finish.
proposals.code: steps(), lines 799-800. const edgeAt = (y) => y > lb - lh*0.3 + 1 ? gx0 - lw*0.32 : y > lb - lh*0.42 + 1 ? gx0 - lw*0.2 : y > lb - lh*0.55 + 1 ? gx0 - lw*0.08 : gx0; for (let y = lb - Y(0.02); y > lb - th + Y(0.01); y -= Y(0.022)) { const xa = y > lb - lh + Y(0.01) ? edgeAt(y) : gx1 - tw2; courses += `M${F(xa + 1)} ${F(y)}H${F(gx1 - 1)}`; }. Line 802: H${F(gx1)} for the string course.

proposals.title: The lookout's warm halo is on before its windows light
proposals.versions: Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night (the one pass)
proposals.observed: The lookout's halo (line 795, radius Y(0.24)) is drawn outside any isl-vwin group, so it is at full strength from the moment the card fades in. The lookout's openings stay dark glass until about 3.6 s (--i 4.6 at a 0.6 s step), so for most of the pass an unlit building sits in a warm glow. The telescope's guardhouse halo, by contrast, is in its --i:2 group.
proposals.proposal: Wrap the halo in the same pass group as the lit openings (isl-vwin isl-vlast, --i:4.6, --isl-vstep .6s), so the glow arrives with the windows and the story ends on the lookout.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.4 treats every light as a set that comes on together, and the owner specified this order himself: the lanterns from the foot to the top, then the lookout's windows.
proposals.code: steps(), line 795: s += `<g class="isl-vwin isl-vlast" style="--i:4.6;--isl-vstep:.6s">${halo(lx, lb - lh*0.45, Y(0.24), 'islvwarm')}</g>`. Keep it before the stone at line 796. The index matches line 860 (lanterns.length + 0.6 = 4.6).

proposals.title: The scrub beside the steps reads as pebbles; make it shrubs
proposals.versions: all five (at Dusk and Night it is the only vegetation on the slope)
proposals.observed: Line 849 scatters flat-bottomed humps 1.4 to 3.2 CSS px across along a line below the stairs. At Dusk and Night they show as small dark dots on the bare slope, reading as pebbles, the exact pattern DESIGN 19.3 warns about. This piece predates the shrubs() helper that the telescope uses.
proposals.proposal: Replace them with five or six shrubs() of about Y(0.03 to 0.045), set along the stair body's lower edge and inside the lanterns' pools. There they are seen against the lighter stone and the lamplight rather than lost on the dark hill.
proposals.why: The owner has already ruled on this: scattered humps read as pebbles, so use shrubs, and put dark scrub where something lighter is behind it. It also gives the empty lower right of the slope a little life at night.
proposals.code: steps(), line 849: s += shrubs(P([[0.4, 0.95], [0.48, 0.83], [0.57, 0.69], [0.7, 0.52], [0.76, 0.42]]).map(([x, y]) => [x + X(0.03), y + Y(0.05), Y(0.038)]), r). This is the last use of r() in steps(), so nothing after it moves. shrubs() is defined at line 880.

proposals.title: The wall's joints come in uneven pairs, one row only, and one spills onto the guardhouse
proposals.versions: all five; the stray joint shows at 1440 (not at 1920), depending on width
proposals.observed: Line 991 staggers alternate joints within one row by Y(0.025): x + (k%2)*Y(0.025). The result is pairs of joints Y(0.025) apart separated by gaps of Y(0.075), not a bond. At 1440 (W 680) the last odd joint lands at 619.6 CSS px, past the wall's end at wx1 = 615.4, so a stray vertical tick is drawn on the guardhouse's face (visible at image x 1239, y 255-268 in both 1440 renders). Only the top course has joints; the course below the joint line is plain.
proposals.proposal: Lay two rows of joints in a true stagger: row 1 (wTop+Y(0.018) to wTop+Y(0.045)) every Y(0.05), and row 2 (wTop+Y(0.045) down to the foot) offset by half. Skip any joint within 1 px of either end of the wall.
proposals.why: It removes a stray line on the building (the kind of stray shape DESIGN 19.5 asks to catch at every width), and the wall then reads as coursed stone all the way down.
proposals.code: telescope(), lines 990-992: for (let row = 0; row < 2; row++) for (let x = wx0 + Y(0.05) - row*Y(0.025); x < wx1 - 1; x += Y(0.05)) if (x > wx0 + 1) wj += `M${F(x)} ${F(wTop + Y(row ? 0.045 : 0.018))}v${F(Y(row ? 0.04 : 0.027))}`. The row-2 joints end under the foot line, which the hill does not cover, so clip them to the foot or keep v at about Y(0.035).

proposals.title: The footpath runs into the face of the wall instead of round its end
proposals.observed: The path's top edge runs from (0.70W, 0.60H) to (0.725W, 0.585H). The wall starts at wx0 = 0.685W and is drawn over it, so the path climbs the hill and stops dead against the wall's face, 5 to 12 CSS px right of the wall's end. The lantern, which the comment places 'at the wall's end, over the path', stands just left of where the path stops.
proposals.proposal: End the path on the hill's brow just past the wall's end, with its top edge from about (0.662W, 0.621H) to (0.684W, 0.600H). Both points lie on the crest line. The path then turns round the end of the wall under the lantern onto the lookout, and the lantern's pool still falls on it.
proposals.why: A path that ends at a blank wall contradicts the scene: the viewer cannot get onto the lookout. This way the lantern marks the way up, as intended.
proposals.code: telescope(), line 943: keep the start and end at the foot of the picture; change the upper segment to ...C X(0.64) Y(0.72) X(0.655) Y(0.645) X(0.662) Y(0.621) L X(0.684) Y(0.6) C X(0.675) Y(0.7) X(0.7) Y(0.86) X(0.665) H+2 Z. The crest points are at line 937 ([0.62,0.68], [0.67,0.61], [0.72,0.575]) and the wall at line 985.

proposals.title: Make the guardhouse read as stone: staggered joints and quoins at its corner
proposals.observed: The comment says 'coursed stone', but the facade has only full-width horizontal lines every Y(0.03) and no vertical joints. At every version it reads as weatherboard siding. Its one visible corner (gx0) is a plain edge.
proposals.proposal: Add short vertical joints in each course band, every Y(0.06) and offset by half on alternate bands, in the same isl-vcourse stroke. Add quoins up the left corner: alternating Y(0.03)/Y(0.02)-wide blocks, one course tall and aligned to the course lines, in isl-vstone at fill-opacity 0.45 (the bell tower's recipe), kept narrow enough to clear the window. The lit window and door, drawn afterwards, cover any joints behind them.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.3 asks for courses and quoins on anything big enough to read. With them the lookout's building matches its stone wall instead of looking like a timber shed.

proposals.title: A shadow under the guardhouse's eave, and shingle courses on its roof
proposals.observed: The roof's eave meets the wall top with no shadow below it; the brown roof sits directly on the tan wall. The roof, described as 'old shingle', is one flat fill.
proposals.proposal: Lay an isl-vpshade band Y(0.03) deep across the wall directly under the eave, from gx0 to the right edge. Add three faint horizontal shingle lines across the roof's front slope, each starting on the hip line at the left.
proposals.why: A shadow cast under an eave is one of the small additions listed for this pass. It separates roof from wall and puts the building in light. The shingle lines give the roof the structure its comment promises.
proposals.code: telescope(): after line 953 add s += `<path class="isl-vpshade" d="${rect(gx0, gTop + 1, X(1.03) - gx0, Y(0.03))}"/>`. After line 954: for k in 1..3, t = k/4, y = gTop + 1 - t*(Y(0.09) + 1), xl = (gx0 - Y(0.02)) + t*((gx0 + (gx1 - gx0)*0.3) - (gx0 - Y(0.02))); sh += `M${F(xl)} ${F(y)}H${F(gx1 + Y(0.1))}`, drawn with class isl-vcourse, stroke-width .7.

proposals.title: The lens reads as a pale ball stuck on the end of the tube
proposals.versions: all five (most by Day, where it is a white dot on blue)
proposals.observed: The objective is a full circle (isl-vlens, r = d0*0.55, about 5.7 CSS px) centred at fx + ux*Y(0.012), just beyond the dew shield's end at fx + ux*Y(0.01). About half the disc stands outside the tube in open sky, so it reads as a ball or a little moon on the tube's end rather than the glass in its mouth. The tube is seen broadside, so its end face should be nearly edge-on.
proposals.proposal: Draw the glass as a thin ellipse filling the dew shield's open end: centred at fx + ux*Y(0.01), rx about Y(0.006) along the tube, ry about d0 across it, rotated to the tube's angle. It becomes a lit rim of glass catching the moonlight, inside the tube's silhouette.
proposals.why: This makes the telescope's one perspective consistent (a tube seen from the side shows its end edge-on) and removes a stray round shape that competes with the real Moon.
proposals.code: telescope(), line 982: `<ellipse class="isl-vlens" cx="${F(fx + ux*Y(0.01))}" cy="${F(fy + uy*Y(0.01))}" rx="${F(Math.max(1, Y(0.006)))}" ry="${F(d0 * 1.0)}" transform="rotate(${F(ang * 180 / Math.PI)} ${F(fx + ux*Y(0.01))} ${F(fy + uy*Y(0.01))})"/>`. ang, ux, uy and d0 are from lines 963-966.

proposals.title: The lit doorway lays a pool of light on the ground
proposals.observed: The guardhouse's arched door is lit (f-pulse) and has the building's large warm halo, but the ground in front of it gets no pool, so the bright door stands on unlit ground.
proposals.proposal: Add a pool at the door's foot, about Y(0.1) wide and Y(0.025) deep and centred just below gBase, in the same --i:2 group as the halo. Draw it before the facade so the building covers its upper half.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.4 treats every light as a set: the light, its halo, and its pool on the ground. A lit doorway that throws light outside grounds the building and adds a last warm touch at the picture's edge.
proposals.code: telescope(), line 952: `<g class="isl-vwin" style="--i:2">${halo(X(0.96), Y(0.46), Y(0.34), 'islvwarm')}${pool(gx0 + (gx1 - gx0)*0.55, gBase + Y(0.015), Y(0.1), Y(0.025), 0.6)}</g>`. dx at line 958 is the same x.

proposals.title: Slivers of sea and sky show between the town's houses
proposals.versions: all five (at Sunset the gaps sit in front of the hidden setting Sun)
proposals.observed: Each house advances x by w + Y(0.01), a 1.9 CSS px gap (3.7 px in the 2x render). The roofs overhang, but below the eaves every gap shows the sea and sky behind as a thin vertical line from the eave to the paving. They are visible at x about 0.38, 0.44, 0.51, 0.57 and 0.66 in every version: blue by Day, pale at Dawn and Dusk.
proposals.proposal: Let the houses stand as a terrace: advance by w - 1, so neighbouring walls overlap by a pixel and no anti-aliased seam opens. Their different wall colours by Day, and their separate gables at night, keep them distinct.
proposals.why: The owner specifically catches 'a gap where the sea shows through'. A 2 px gap does not read as an alley; it reads as a seam.
proposals.code: bellTower(), line 2112: x += w - 1 (was w + Y(0.01)). The loop may fit one more house before X(0.66). The houses are the last users of r() in this function, and the last house still ends well left of the tower (b0 is about 0.767W).

proposals.title: The quoins stick out of the tower as see-through blocks and are out of step with the courses
proposals.observed: (a) The right-hand quoins' x values are swapped against their widths. The odd ones start at t1 - Y(0.05) with width Y(0.066), so they overshoot the shaft by Y(0.016), about 3 CSS px. The even ones stop 3 px short of the corner. The overshoot is isl-vstone at fill-opacity 0.45, so it is a translucent block over the sea and sky, giving a ragged sawtooth right edge (the left edge is straight). (b) The quoins step every Y(0.045) while the courses step every Y(0.05), so quoin joints and course lines drift apart up the shaft. (c) The last quoins start at 155.3 CSS px with height 7.4, ending about 3 px below the ground line (160) over the paving.
proposals.proposal: Make each quoin exactly one course tall, on the course lines (step Y(0.05)), alternately long and short, flush with both corners (x = t0 on the left, t1 - width on the right). Fill the part course left at the foot (0.83H to 0.86H) with a plinth: a base course slightly wider than the shaft, in isl-vstone, so the tower visibly stands on the square.
proposals.why: Quoins and courses that line up are what make stone read as stone, and the owner looks for parts out of rhythm. See-through blocks over the sea and a ragged silhouette are the kind of stray shape he rejects. The plinth is a small contact detail that grounds the tower.
proposals.code: bellTower(), line 2138: const cs = Y(0.05); for (let y = tTop, k = 0; y + cs <= ground + 0.5; y += cs, k++) { const qw = Y(k % 2 ? 0.07 : 0.05); qn += rect(t0, y + 0.6, qw, cs - 1.2) + rect(t1 - qw, y + 0.6, qw, cs - 1.2); }. After line 2139: s += `<path class="isl-vstone" d="${rect(t0 - Y(0.012), ground - Y(0.03), tw + Y(0.024), Y(0.03) + 1)}"/>`. The course loop at line 2137 is unchanged.

proposals.title: The shaft shows a shaded side face that the belfry and roof do not have
proposals.observed: The shaft's right 30% (tc + 0.2tw to t1) is shaded as a side face from the ground up to the lower cornice, then stops. The belfry stage, both cornices and the pyramid roof above are flat and centred, and the arch, bell, roof apex and vane all sit on the centre line tc. This is the Court House symptom (a side face stopping at the cornice). It cannot be carried up, though: a side face from tc + 0.2tw would cut through the arch opening, whose right jamb is at tc + 0.32tw, putting the opening on the edge between two faces.
proposals.proposal: Treat the tower as seen straight on, as the owner decided for the campus clock tower today: remove the shaft's side shade. Keep the modelling with the one shade that fits a straight-on view, a shadow cast under the belfry's lower cornice across the full width of the shaft (about Y(0.03) deep, isl-vpshade). Together with islvfacade's darkening toward the top, that keeps the tower from looking flat. If he prefers the side, the alternative is to move the arch, bell and roof apex left onto the centre of the front face and carry the shade through the belfry, both cornices and the roof's right half, a larger change.
proposals.why: Lit and shaded planes must follow real faces of the form (DESIGN 19.3). The owner judged the clock tower's side shade 'subtly off' on a building meant to be seen straight on, and this tower is drawn the same way. Removing the shade is a one-line change that can be backed out in one step.
proposals.code: bellTower(), line 2135: drop the `<path class="isl-vpshade" d="${rect(tc + tw*0.2, ...)}"/>`. Add after line 2143 (the cornices): s += `<path class="isl-vpshade" d="${rect(t0, tTop + Y(0.012), tw, Y(0.03))}"/>`.

proposals.title: The weather vane is drawn above the picture; only a clipped rod shows
proposals.observed: roofTop = Y(0.005), about 0.9 CSS px. The rod runs up to roofTop - Y(0.03), about -4.7 px (clipped), the compass bar sits at y 0 (half cut) and the vane's flag spans y -4.7 to -2.0, wholly outside the frame. What reads is a thin rod running out of the top of the card like an antenna, with a cut bar.
proposals.proposal: Bring the whole finial inside the frame above the roof's apex, which stays at Y(0.045). Run the rod to about Y(0.007), put the flag at Y(0.007) to Y(0.02) pointing downwind, and put the compass bar at about Y(0.03). If that is too cramped at 1440, drop the bar and keep the rod and flag whole.
proposals.why: The comment promises a vane and the drawing never shows it. A detail cut by the frame edge is exactly the kind of awkward clip the owner notices at the top of a card.

proposals.title: Give the sea its finish: horizon hatch and the headland's reflection
proposals.observed: The sea band between the horizon (0.72H) and the square (0.86H) has only build()'s generic ripples. Unlike every other harbour piece, bellTower() adds no hatchList ripples dense at the horizon, and the far headland has rim and mist but no mirrored reflection. The water left of the palms and around the tower reads thin next to the telescope's and the steps'.
proposals.proposal: Add the standard finish: hatchList dashes from y0 to the ground line (drawn first, so the town covers most of it) and mirrored(y0, farLand, 0.18) under the headland. Use a separate random stream so the town's houses keep exactly their present sizes.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.3 lists the hatch for every sea or harbour and reflections of land at the waterline. Both are already-approved finish, applied where this piece skipped them.
proposals.code: bellTower(), after line 2101: const rs = rng(733); s += dashes(hatchList(W, y0, ground, rs), 's-vrip', 1, [0.1, 0.18, 0.28]) + mirrored(y0, farLand, 0.18). Using rs, not r, avoids shifting the house loop's r() sequence at lines 2110-2116.

proposals.title: The notice board's little roof merges with the house roofs behind it
proposals.versions: all five (merged into one silhouette at Dawn, Dusk and Night; red on red by Day)
proposals.observed: The board's roof uses isl-troof, the town's roof class: --isl-far at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk and Night, and the same terracotta by Day. It sits directly in front of a house gable, so at Dusk and Night the two form one dark shape, and by Day it is red against red. The roof no longer reads as part of the notice board, the object that ties the picture to Announcements.
proposals.proposal: Draw the board's roof in the board's own dark joinery wood (isl-lwood2, as its frame), so board and roof read as one piece of furniture in every version and stand clear of the house silhouettes behind.
proposals.why: The at-a-glance tie to the page title depends on the notice board reading cleanly. This is a one-class change, and the token already exists in all five versions.
proposals.code: bellTower(), line 2174: class="isl-lwood2" instead of "isl-troof". The tokens are in layout-art.css lines 446, 455, 464, 473 and 482.

proposals.title: Pave the square in perspective, as the Way In picture does
proposals.observed: The 'square's paving' is the near-land fill (f-near, green grass by Day) crossed by parallel diagonal hatch lines all slanting the same way. At Dusk and Night they read as rain streaks, and by Day as mown grass, not paving.
proposals.proposal: Reuse wayIn()'s approved paving: an isl-apave fill (stone grey by Day, deep slate at night), horizontal joints that widen toward the viewer, and joint lines converging toward the middle of the horizon. The square then recedes under the tower, the board and the lantern, whose pool lies on stone.
proposals.why: The picture gets one true perspective and a surface that matches its description. The idiom and its five-version tokens already exist in the file.
proposals.code: bellTower(), lines 2127-2130 become: s += `<path class="isl-apave" d="${rect(-2, ground, W + 4, H - ground + 2)}"/>`; for (let y = ground + Y(0.035); y < H; y += Y(0.04) + (y - ground)*0.2) pav += `M-2 ${F(y)}H${F(W + 2)}`; for (let x = X(0.01); x < W; x += Y(0.09)) pav += `M${F(x)} ${F(ground)}l${F((x - W*0.5)*0.08)} ${F(H - ground)}`; s += `<path class="isl-vcourse" d="${pav}" stroke-width=".7" stroke-opacity=".5"/>`. The precedent is wayIn() at lines 2709-2713 and layout-art.css lines 688-700.

checked_fine: Read DESIGN.md 19 in full; the code for steps(), telescope() and bellTower(), their PIECES entries and build(); and the CSS for every class they use. All 13 renders per piece were opened.

All three: every H and V command in these functions takes one number (checked by reading); every light group uses isl-vwin with an ordered --i; halos and pools clear by Day through --isl-g1 being transparent, and lamps show unlit (isl-vlamp is --isl-vdark by Day).
Lamp-lit steps: the lanterns come on from the foot up (--i 0 to 3, --isl-vstep .6s), then the lookout's openings (--i 4.6, isl-vlast), as the owner specified.

Lamp-lit steps: every lantern has its halo and its pool; the foot lantern stands on land about 15 CSS px inside the shore; the landing lanterns stand on their landings and the top one on the top tread; the top lantern is the only kind-hue accent.

Lamp-lit steps: the lookout's openings are dark glass by Day; its base sits into the crest along most of its width; the turret's shade carries up through the merlons (apart from the crenel spill in lamp-steps-2).

Lamp-lit steps: the Sunset Sun sits in clear sky just left of where the slope meets the sea, with its path drawn under the land; at Night there is no rim or glow and the stars come down to the crest; the far shore is mirrored and misted.
Lamp-lit steps: the Day trees stay whole on the land; the 1440 composition keeps its shapes.

Telescope: the tripod's feet are hidden behind the wall; the lantern stands on the coping in the page's hue, with its halo and pool, and comes on last (--i:4, isl-vlast) after the harbour (--i:0) and the guardhouse (--i:2).
Telescope: all five boats have hull, mast, masthead light, column of light and reflection; the far hills are rimmed on the sunset side, mirrored and misted.
Telescope: the Sunset Sun at 18:02 rests on the far range's summit with its path on the open sea; the tube is aimed up and to the left, toward the Moon's side of the sky, not at the harbour.

Telescope: the wall abuts the guardhouse with no gap; the hipped roof reads correctly as its trapezoid front slope seen straight on; the shrubs use the shared helper, whose base is wound the same way as the crowns; the 1920 and 1440 compositions hold.
Bell tower: the bell swings mouth-right under its beam while the clapper hangs plumb (checked the rotate(-22) arithmetic).

Bell tower: the belfry opening is cut evenodd, so sky and stars show through it; the three rings spread in turn (--i 1 to 3) and the lantern lights last (--i:4, isl-vlast), with its halo and its pool on the square.

Bell tower: the kind hue appears only in the lantern and its halo; the palm trunks are brown by Day; the notes, pins and ink lines read at size; the town's windows are glass by Day and lit from Dawn to Night.
Bell tower: at Sunset the Sun is set behind the town, so neither disc nor path shows, which is consistent (the gaps in bell-tower-1 are the only place it could leak through).
No Moon is drawn in any render, which is correct when it is not up at the render moment; each piece keeps open sky at its moonX for the nights it is.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. At Dusk and Night twelve columns of light run down from a far shore with no light points on it, and steps() never draws an s-vlight path for shoreLights (lines 760-763). By Day, the houses on the right-hand end stand at 0.582-0.596H while the shore's top falls to about 0.598H, so they sit on a sliver of land or just above it. The proposed topAt(x) placement keeps the two r() calls per light, so the random stream is unchanged, and lightsD and s-vlight (hidden by Day, css line 155) are already in scope. The owner treats a light as a set, and this is the only piece where the water carries reflections of lights that are not there.

Confirmed in both renders and code. The slit spans gx1-12.9 to gx1-9.9 px and the shade starts at gx1-10.3, so it straddles the edge between the faces. The shade rectangle runs up to the merlon tops, so the crenels at the turret's top right show a translucent teal block over the sky by Day and a dark, starless patch at Night (night right-half 3x, top right). This is today's Betty's Hope and Court House lessons in one small repair, and the arithmetic in the proposal checks out: the lit face's centre is gx1 - 0.725*tw2, and merlons of tw2/5 placed at 0, 0.4 and 0.8 of tw2 put one on each corner. If the owner reads the lookout as seen straight on, like the clock tower, the one-step alternative is to drop the turret shade and keep the slit centred.

Confirmed at 3x (dusk right half, around x 405-445, y 383-515). The landing lantern's glass and post are painted over the agave's lower left branches, although the stalk passes in front of the treads, so the draw order contradicts the depth. At real size it is subtle, which is why the value is low. Moving it X(0.03) clears the lantern. One interaction to watch: after the move, the rosette's right leaves reach about (0.73W, 0.57H), which is exactly where lamp-steps-7 puts a shrub. If both are adopted, use the shrub positions in lamp-steps-7's revision, which keep clear of the plant.

Confirmed. The yacht has no reflection, while the telescope's boats and the regatta do, and DESIGN 19.3 asks for one under every hull. The mast with two symmetrical stays and no boom does read as an A-frame. The mirrored group is the same idiom the telescope uses, and no r() calls are added. A boom with a furled sail (one pale stroke) is a small, true detail. It can be combined with the missed item below that raises the masthead: build the mirrored copy from the final rig.

Confirmed. The broken wall is a plain pale block with no courses, next to the coursed lookout (day and dusk right halves, x 700-810). The turret's top 0.22*lh above the parapet is also plain. The edgeAt() steps in the proposal match the wall polygon at line 794 (0.3, 0.42 and 0.55 of lh). Keeping the same stroke and spacing adds structure without clutter, and it carries the Court House idea of running the structure round the whole form.

Confirmed in code: the Y(0.24) warm halo at line 795 is outside any isl-vwin group, so it is at full strength while the lookout's openings are dark glass until about 3.6 s (0.8 + 4.6*0.6, css line 946). Wrapping it in the same --i:4.6 / .6s group completes the set the owner described (the lanterns from the foot, then the lookout). Two isl-vlast elements with the same timing are already used elsewhere (lines 1327-1329), so the end-of-pass hook is unaffected. By Day, isl-vwin is not animated.

Confirmed. At Dusk and Night the humps from line 849 (1.4 to 3.2 px) show as small dark dots scattered down the bare slope (night right-half 3x at about (735,497), (523,633), (262,779), (190,830)), which is the pebble pattern the owner has ruled out. But the proposed positions (0.43,1.0), (0.51,0.88), (0.6,0.74), (0.73,0.57), (0.79,0.47) lie 0.05-0.07H below the stair body, on the dark hill, which contradicts the proposal's own aim of setting them against lighter stone. The one at (0.73,0.57) also collides with the agave's rosette if lamp-steps-3 moves it.
verdicts.revised_proposal: Replace line 849 with four shrubs whose feet sit just below the stair body's lower edge, so each dark crown overlaps the lighter stone and the edge of a lantern's pool: shrubs(P([[0.41, 0.915], [0.49, 0.82], [0.57, 0.72], [0.76, 0.42]]).map(([x, y]) => [x, y, Y(0.036)]), r). The body's lower edge is at about 0.907H at x 0.41, 0.807H under the first landing, 0.708H at x 0.57 and 0.408H at x 0.76. These positions stay clear of the agave in either position (its leaves reach from 0.611W to 0.737W) and of the lantern posts. It remains the last use of r(), so nothing else moves.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed by arithmetic and in the render. At 1440 (W 680) the last odd joint lands at 619.6 CSS px, beyond wx1 = 615.4, and it is visible as a short tick on the guardhouse face (1440 day and dusk whole, x about 1239, y 255-268), because the facade is drawn before the wall's joints. The (k%2)*Y(0.025) offset inside one row produces pairs of joints, not a bond (visible at 3x). Two staggered rows with an end guard fix the stray line and give the wall a true bond. Keeping the row-2 joints at about Y(0.035-0.04) keeps them above the foot, which is at least 0.585H.

At real size the path's top already goes behind the low wall a few pixels right of its end, directly under the lantern and inside its pool (dusk and night right halves, x 510-600, y 480-510). That reads as the way up to the lookout, which is the intent. The proposed end, a top edge from (0.662,0.621) to (0.684,0.600), lies on the crest exactly where it meets the horizon (y0 = 0.62H) against the sea and sky, so the path's top would sit on the skyline at the water's edge and risk reading as a path running off the brow. The gain is doubtful and the change could introduce a new oddity.

Confirmed. The guardhouse has only full-width horizontal lines every Y(0.03) and no vertical joints, so at Dusk and Sunset in particular it reads as clapboard siding, not the 'coursed stone' its comment promises. Staggered joints and quoins on the one visible corner are the DESIGN 19.3 structure. However, the proposed Y(0.03) quoin ends 1.4 CSS px short of the window (which starts at gx0 + Y(0.035)), which would look cramped.
verdicts.revised_proposal: As proposed (running-bond joints every Y(0.06) in each Y(0.03) band, offset by half on alternate bands, in isl-vcourse .7, drawn before the door and window so they cover the joints), but make the quoins narrower, alternating Y(0.022) and Y(0.014) wide, one course tall and aligned to the course lines, in isl-vstone at fill-opacity .45, so there is a clear gap of at least 3 px before the window.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. The brown roof sits directly on the wall with no shadow under the eave in any version (day right-half 3x, x 1040-1280, y 270). A band of isl-vpshade under the eave has a direct precedent in the Way In's parapet shadow (line 2727), and it separates roof from wall. The shingle lines are faint and add little, especially at Night on a dark roof. They are harmless, but most of the value is the eave shadow, so ship that first if only one part goes in.

Confirmed. isl-vlens is filled with --isl-moon at 0.8 (css line 857), a disc of radius about 5.7 px centred just beyond the dew shield, so half of it stands in open sky. In every version it reads as a pale ball or a small Moon on the end of the tube (day and dusk right halves, about (645,160)). That matters because the owner keeps the Moon to nights when it is really up. An edge-on ellipse is right, but at Y(0.006) (about 1.6 px wide) it may vanish at real size, and the glass would stop reading at all.
verdicts.revised_proposal: Replace the circle with an ellipse centred on the dew shield's mouth (fx + ux*Y(0.01), fy + uy*Y(0.01)), rotated to the tube's angle (ang in degrees), with rx about d0*0.3 along the tube (about 3 CSS px) and ry about d0 across it. It then reads as the lit glass of the objective seen nearly edge-on, fills the mouth instead of standing off it, and no longer reads as a second Moon.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. The lit arched door stands on unlit ground; only the building's large halo reaches it (night right-half 3x, x 1195-1235, y 455). DESIGN 19.4 treats a light as a set (light, halo, pool). Putting the pool in the existing --i:2 group, drawn before the facade so the building covers its upper half, is a one-line addition, and nothing is near it (the nearest shrub foot is at 0.71H or lower).

Confirmed in every version at both widths. The Y(0.01) (1.9 px) gaps between houses show the sea and sky as thin seams from eave to paving: blue by Day, pale at Dawn and Dusk, and lit by the afterglow at Sunset (for example 1920 whole at x 625, 710, 832 and 937; 1440 day at 531 and 609). The owner explicitly catches the sea showing through a gap. But 'x += w - 1' changes the loop's house count, and every roof peak comes from r() calls made after the loop, so all the gables and the whole approved street would shift.
verdicts.revised_proposal: Keep the layout and the r() stream exactly, and close each seam by widening each house's wall rectangle by the gap: at line 2115, walls[i % 3] += rect(hx, top, w + Y(0.01) + 0.5, ground - top + 1). The roof's eave overhangs by Y(0.015), so it still covers the widened corner, the windows and roofs are unchanged, and the houses become a terrace with no seams.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed by arithmetic and at 3x (day right half, x 874-920). The right-hand quoins' x values are swapped against their widths, so alternate blocks overshoot the shaft by Y(0.016) (about 3 px) as translucent stone over the sea and sky, and the rest stop 3 px short: a ragged right edge beside a straight left one. The Y(0.045) quoin step drifts against the Y(0.05) courses, and the last quoins end about 3 px below the ground line on the grass. The proposed loop places quoins one course tall on the course lines, flush at both corners, with the last partial course (0.83H to 0.86H) filled by a plinth. The arithmetic checks out, and it is a clear, small correction of the kind the owner catches.

Confirmed. The shaft's right 30% is shaded as a side face from the ground to the lower cornice and then stops, while the belfry, the cornices, the roof, the arch, the bell and the vane are all drawn straight on around tc. That is the Court House symptom, and it cannot be carried up without putting the arch on the edge between faces (right jamb at tc+0.32tw, shade from tc+0.2tw). The quoins at t1 also mark t1 as the front face's corner, which contradicts a side face beginning at tc+0.2tw. Removing the shade follows today's clock-tower ruling exactly, and the shadow under the cornice keeps the tower from looking flat. It can be backed out in one step.

Confirmed. roofTop is Y(0.005). The rod runs to about -4.6 px, the bar sits at y 0 and is half cut, and the vane's flag (y -4.6 to -2) is entirely outside the frame, so what reads is a rod and a cut bar at the card's top edge, somewhat like a clipped cross (day, dusk and night right halves, and 1440). But the proposed flag at Y(0.007) runs 1.3 px from the frame edge, with the bar squeezed in between, which would look cramped against the edge.
verdicts.revised_proposal: Drop the compass bar and fit a small vane fully inside the frame with a margin: the rod from the apex (Y(0.045)) up to Y(0.012), and the flag from Y(0.012) to Y(0.025) pointing right as now (M tc Y(0.012) h Y(0.04) l -Y(0.01) Y(0.013) h -Y(0.03) Z). Check it at 1440 and 1280, where H changes.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed. The sea strip (0.72H to 0.86H) left of the palms and right of the tower has only a few generic ripples (dusk left-half 3x), and the headland has a rim and mist but no reflection, unlike the other harbour pieces and DESIGN 19.3's 'every sea or harbour'. hatchList and mirrored are in scope, and a separate rng(733) keeps the houses' r() stream intact. The strip is thin, so the gain is modest, but the headland's reflection is a nice finish.

Confirmed. The board's roof uses isl-troof, which is --isl-far at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk and Night (css line 226). It sits right in front of a house gable of the same class and merges with it into one silhouette (dusk and night right halves, x 320-560, y 282-310), and by Day it is terracotta on terracotta. isl-lwood2 exists in all five versions (lines 446-482), and at Dusk the frame in that token already stands clear of the navy houses. A one-class change that keeps the object tied to Announcements reading cleanly.

Confirmed. The 'square's paving' is the f-near fill (green by Day) crossed by parallel diagonal strokes that all slant the same way. By Day they read as mown grass, and at Dusk and Night as rain streaks (dusk left half, the foreground band). wayIn()'s isl-apave fill with widening joints and converging lines is an approved idiom with tokens in all five versions (css lines 688-700). Because it changes the whole foreground band's colour in every version, present it to the owner as an option rather than a quiet fix. Also check the tower's plinth (bell-tower-2) against the paving by Day, since #b9b2a3 paving is close to the stone.

missed.title: The yacht's masthead light sits exactly on the horizon
missed.observed: The mast runs to by - Y(0.2) = Y(0.8) - Y(0.2) = Y(0.6), and the piece's horizon is 0.6 (PIECES 'lamp-steps', horizon: 0.6), so the tip of the mast, the riding light and its halo sit exactly on the horizon line, at the foot of the far shore. In every render the mast's tip touches the horizon (a tangent), and at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk and Night the riding light reads as one more light at the shore's waterline rather than the light at the top of the yacht's mast (night left-half 3x at (463,613); 1440 dusk at (258,341)).
missed.proposal: Raise the mast so the masthead stands clear in the sky above the far shore: mast to by - Y(0.25), so the light is at 0.55H, about 10 CSS px above the far shore's crest (about 0.58H at x 0.19). Move the halo, the riding light and the tops of both stays with it. A sloop's mast is taller than its hull, so the boat also reads more clearly as a yacht. If lamp-steps-4 is adopted, build its reflection from the raised rig.
missed.why: A tangent between a mast's tip and the horizon is the kind of small misalignment the owner catches, and it makes the one boat's light indistinguishable from the shore's. Standing the light clear gives the yacht its own light and its column a clear source.
missed.code: steps(), lines 767 and 770: replace Y(0.2) with Y(0.25) in the halo, the f-pulse circle and the mast's V; replace Y(0.19) with Y(0.24) at the stays' top. No r() calls change. The column of light at line 766 is unchanged.

proposals.title: The Sunset clock shows two hour hands
proposals.observed: At Sunset the clock face carries three hands: the 18:30 hour hand (just left of straight down), a second hour hand at the 7:30 position, and the minute hand straight down. The dusk hand ('isl-d', 19:30) is drawn at Sunset too, because layout-art.css hides .isl-d only at Night, Dawn and Day (lines 68-70, 118). .isl-d is meant to show at Sunset (for the Moon), so the clock is the one drawing where it leaks.
proposals.proposal: Show each hand in its own version only. Put the Dusk hand in the library's per-version group, <g class="isl-lq" data-q="d">, which shows only at Dusk. Keep isl-a, isl-y and isl-s as they are, and keep isl-n for Night. A CSS alternative: .isl[data-sky="sunset"] .isl-chand.isl-d { display: none; }.
proposals.why: A clock with two hour hands contradicts itself, and it is the clock the caption's time of day depends on. The owner would read it as 'two times at once'.
proposals.code: weekCalendar, lines 2275-2277: in the loop over [['isl-a',6,5],['isl-y',10,30],['isl-s',18,30],['isl-d',19,30],['isl-n',22,0]], wrap the 'isl-d' path, e.g. const p = `<path class="${cls === 'isl-d' ? '' : cls} isl-chand" .../>`; s += cls === 'isl-d' ? `<g class="isl-lq" data-q="d">${p}</g>` : p;. Uses the existing .isl-lq / data-q rules (layout-art.css 528-532). No rng use, so nothing else shifts.

proposals.title: The potted plant is drawn in the landscape's night colour
proposals.versions: Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night (Day is right)
proposals.observed: The shelf plant comes from shrubs(), which returns the outdoor classes 'f-near isl-shrub' and 'isl-vlit isl-shrubl'. Only Day retints them to vegetation (layout-art.css 242-243), so in the other four versions the crown takes --isl-near, the far-shore silhouette colour: navy at Dawn and Sunset and near-black at Dusk and Night. It reads as a dark blob beside a cream calendar and a lit mug, the darkest thing in a lamp-lit room.
proposals.proposal: Give the plant a room green in every version, as the other indoor objects have material tokens. Swap the crown's class to the library's shade green (--isl-lshade: #1f5e3e Dawn, #1f5f3c Sunset, #1e5a3a Dusk, #143d27 Night), keeping 'isl-shrub' so Day's more specific rule still gives it the vegetation green. Optionally tint the lit crown with --isl-lglow0 at low opacity in place of the blue-grey --isl-vlit.
proposals.why: Buildings and objects are meant to be identical in every version, with only light changing. Here the plant turns from a plant into a navy silhouette whenever it is not Day. The owner's caution that dark on dark disappears applies too: at Night it has no form left.
proposals.code: weekCalendar line 2288: shrubs([...], r).replace('f-near isl-shrub', 'isl-tshade isl-shrub'). .isl-tshade already maps to var(--isl-lshade) (layout-art.css 587), and .isl[data-sky=day] .isl-shrub (0,3,0) outranks .isl .isl-tshade (0,2,0), so Day is unchanged. The shrubs() call and its r() draws stay as they are.

proposals.title: Event dots collide with a crossed-off day and the ring
proposals.observed: The event dot at cell [2,2] (red, the third day of this week) sits at (0.72, 0.30) of its cell, exactly on the anti-diagonal of that day's X, so it peeks out from under the cross stroke as a smudge. The dot at [5,3] sits 0.3 of a row below the ringed week: its top (0.0156H below the row line) runs under the ring's stroke (0.004H to 0.020H), so it is tucked under the ring's lower edge (visible at 3x day: blue dot touching the ring).
proposals.proposal: Move [2,2] to [5,2], an event later this week inside the ring after today's circle. It then reads as 'what's coming this week', a small addition to the page's story. Move [5,3] one row down to [5,4] (or any row-4 cell) so no dot touches the ring.
proposals.why: Two things touching by accident read as mistakes at 1920. The calendar's point is the ringed week, so its edges and crosses should be clean. A coming event inside the ring ties the picture closer to 'This Week'.
proposals.code: weekCalendar line 2256: the list [[1,0,'isl-lbk2'],[4,1,'isl-lbk3'],[2,2,'isl-lbk1'],[5,3,'isl-lbk2'],[0,4,'isl-lbk3'],[6,1,'isl-lbk1']] becomes [..., [5,2,'isl-lbk1'], [5,4,'isl-lbk2'], ...]. Check: [5,2] centre at wy+0.3gh, top 0.0156H below the row line, clear of the ring's top stroke, which lies above the line. No rng use.

proposals.title: Calendar and clock shadows fall toward the lights
proposals.observed: The calendar's drop shadow (isl-tdrop) is offset right and down, so a dark strip about 4 CSS px wide runs down the calendar's right edge. That is exactly where the sconce's warm halo falls at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk and Night, and it is the side facing the window by Day. The clock's shadow is offset the same way, a crescent at its lower right. Every light in the room (the window and the sconce) is to the right.
proposals.proposal: Mirror the horizontal offsets so the shadows fall down and to the left, away from the sconce and the window. Keep the shelf's straight-down shadow.
proposals.why: The owner's rule: light must come from the scene's own source. A shadow inside the lamp's own halo reads as wrong at once, and the flip costs nothing. (The tool wall's pegboard shadow, line 1877, is offset right the same way, but only about 0.75 px of it shows beyond the frame, so it can stay.)
proposals.code: weekCalendar line 2246: rect(cx0 + Y(0.012), cT + Y(0.02), cw, cB - cT) -> rect(cx0 - Y(0.012), cT + Y(0.02), cw, cB - cT). Line 2269: cx="${F(kx + Y(0.01))}" -> cx="${F(kx - Y(0.01))}" on the isl-tdrop circle.

proposals.title: The sconce's own light: the lit mouth under its shade
proposals.versions: Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night (the lamp is off by Day)
proposals.observed: When lit, the sconce has a warm halo and a cone of light down the wall, but no light source: the shade stays a dark bronze bucket with nothing glowing under it. The tool wall's lamp (isl-tbulb ellipse) and the desk lamp (isl-tbulb circle) both show their bulbs. The cone's bottom half-width, Y(0.12), also carries it about 13 px across the window's lower-left glass, where it reads as haze over the view.
proposals.proposal: Add the lit opening under the shade: a warm ellipse (isl-tbulb) at the shade's mouth, half covered by the shade so its lower half glows, inside the lit group so it comes on in the pass and is absent by Day. Optionally narrow the cone's foot to about Y(0.07) so it stays on the wall between the calendar and the window frame.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.4: every light is a set (the light itself, its halo, its pool or column). Here the light itself is missing, so the halo seems to come from nowhere. The fix matches the room's other lamps.
proposals.code: weekCalendar line 2291, inside <g class="isl-vlamps isl-vwin" style="--i:1"> before the shade (line 2292): + `<ellipse class="isl-tbulb" cx="${F(lx)}" cy="${F(ly + Y(0.07))}" rx="${F(Y(0.026))}" ry="${F(Y(0.008))}"/>`. Cone: the polygon's [lx ± Y(0.12), Y(0.62)] -> [lx ± Y(0.07), Y(0.62)]. Check 1440 and 1280, where the window and calendar move.

proposals.title: Faint reflections under the boats in the window
proposals.versions: all five (shared windowView, so also the hospital room and the committee room)
proposals.observed: The two boats at anchor in windowView have hulls, masts, masthead lights and columns, but no reflections. The far land is mirrored (mirrored(y0, farLand, 0.16)), and the tool wall's boats each carry a faint mirrored hull and mast (toolWall line 1861).
proposals.proposal: Mirror each boat's hull and mast about its own waterline at 0.15 opacity, as the tool wall does. The wall drawn after windowView already hides any reflection that runs below the window.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.3 lists a reflection for every hull and sail, and the tool wall already does this. It makes the boats sit on the water instead of on it like cut-outs, and it is consistent across the three news interiors.
proposals.code: windowView, lines 2213-2219: const hull = `M...Z` (the existing hull string); after the streak: s += `<g opacity=".15"><g transform="translate(0 ${F(2 * by)}) scale(1 -1)"><path class="isl-vhull" d="${hull}"/><path class="isl-vmast" d="M${F(bx)} ${F(by)}V${F(by - mh)}" stroke-width=".8"/></g></g>`;. No rng use, so the random lights do not move.

proposals.title: The middle boat hides behind the window's mullion
proposals.versions: all five (its light and column at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night); same at 1440
proposals.observed: The middle boat is placed at fx 0.5 of the window, exactly where the mullion stands (wx0 + ww*0.5). Its mast and masthead light are hidden behind the bar, but its forestay, its hull and its column of light on the water still show. At Dusk and Night there is a broken column of light under the mullion with no light above it.
proposals.proposal: Move the boat off the mullion to about fx 0.4, into the left pane's open water (clear of the boat at 0.2, and of the Moon's pane above, since its mast top stays below the transom).
proposals.why: A light column with no light, and a boat whose mast is missing, are what the owner catches. DESIGN 19.4: every light is a set.
proposals.code: toolWall line 1854: [[0.2, 0.1, 0.9], [0.5, 0.06, 0.7], [0.78, 0.13, 1.1]] -> [0.4, 0.06, 0.7]. The number of r() calls is unchanged, so nothing else moves.

proposals.title: The window's reveal is on the wrong jamb
proposals.observed: The shaded reveal strip (isl-lsidew) runs down the LEFT inside edge of the window. The window is at the right of the picture, so the viewer stands to its left and can see only its RIGHT jamb (the face turned toward them). The left jamb faces away and could only be seen from the right of the window. The news interiors draw it this way: windowWall with side 1 for a right-hand window (week calendar, hospital room), side -1 for the committee room's left-hand window.
proposals.proposal: Draw the jamb strip on the window's right edge (the mitred strip from wx1 inward). Keep the sill strip.
proposals.why: This is the same kind of fix as the clock tower and the mill doors: a face drawn that the rest of the drawing says cannot be seen. It also makes the tool wall agree with the four later window pictures.
proposals.code: toolWall line 1869: polyD([[wx0, wT], [wx0 + rv, wT + rv], [wx0 + rv, wB], [wx0, wB]]) -> polyD([[wx1, wT], [wx1 - rv, wT + rv], [wx1 - rv, wB], [wx1, wB]]). Equivalently, lines 1867-1872 could become windowWall(W, H, toolFrame(W, H), 'isltwallg', 1), with the duplicate gradient def at line 1843 dropped.

proposals.title: The transom bar crosses the top of the setting Sun
proposals.observed: At 18:23 the Sun is 1.68 degrees up (SKY.sunset). In this short card (H about 186 CSS px at 1920) its disc spans y 54.6 to 73.3, while the transom stands at 59.2 (±1 px), so the bar cuts off the top quarter of the disc. At 1440 the Sun (51.8 to 67.4) still meets the bar (52.8 to 54.8). The Moon's pane above rules out raising the transom here.
proposals.proposal: Give the tool wall its own later minute, 18:26 (1.07 degrees up). The disc (62.6 to 81.3 at 1920, 58.5 to 74.1 at 1440) then clears the bar and settles a quarter of the way into the far hill, with its path still on the water. If it should stand fully on the hill, also turn the view so the Sun falls at about 0.85 to 0.9 of the window, where the hill is lower.
proposals.why: The owner wants the Sun soft, whole and in a clear sky, never with a wisp across it. A window bar across its crown reads the same way. The news windows are taller and are fine at 18:23.
proposals.code: PIECES['tool-wall'] (line 2993): sunset: '18:23' -> '18:26', and update its comment. Optional: in face (line 2995) change f.ww * 0.7 to f.ww * 0.86. Re-render Sunset at 1920, 1440, 1280 and 1120.

proposals.title: A rack for the screwdrivers and chisels, a peg for the tape
proposals.observed: Each tool group gets one hook, at its centre top. The middle screwdriver and the middle chisel hang from it, but the outer screwdrivers and the outer chisels hang from nothing, and the tape measure hangs by its clip below the chisels with no peg at all.
proposals.proposal: Give the drivers and the chisels the rack a real shadow board uses: a short wooden bar across each group, just under the ferrules, with the shafts or blades passing through it, drawn over the tools. Drop the centre hook for those two groups. Add a short peg above the tape's clip, between the middle chisel's tip and the clip.
proposals.why: On a shadow board every tool visibly hangs on something. This is a small true detail in the spirit of the Court House corner, and it removes three floating tools.
proposals.code: toolWall loop, lines 1887-1899: const rack = { drivers: [0.225, 0.14], chiseltape: [0.168, 0.125] }[k]; if (rack) board += `<path class="isl-lwood" transform="${at}" d="${rect(-rack[1] * ts, rack[0] * ts, 2 * rack[1] * ts, 0.03 * ts)}"/>`; else hooks += (existing hook). Tape peg: if (k === 'chiseltape') hooks += `M${F(cx)} ${F(top + 0.39 * ts)}v${F(0.05 * ts)}`. The ferrules sit at 0.195 to 0.225 (drivers) and 0.145 to 0.167 (chisels) of ts. There the peg sits clear of the painted outlines. No rng use.

proposals.title: The hammer on the bench: the outline's hammer, resting on its claw
proposals.versions: Dawn, Day, Sunset, Dusk (the isl-lq 'aysd' group)
proposals.observed: The bench hammer is a handle lying flat on the bench, joined to the FOOT of an upright head, like a boot. Its claw flares away from the handle. On the board's hammer (and on any claw hammer) the handle enters the head's middle and the claw curls back toward the handle.
proposals.proposal: Draw the bench hammer from the board hammer's own parts (TOOLS.hammer(u)), turned about 76 degrees. It then rests as a claw hammer set down does: on its claw tip and the butt of its handle, the face up, the handle sloping gently to the bench. It is the same shape as the empty outline above it.
proposals.why: The day version's story is 'the hammer is out of its outline, on the bench'. Using the outline's own shape makes that read at a glance, and it fixes the claw's direction.
proposals.code: toolWall lines 1923-1925: const hm = TOOLS.hammer(u); const hammerFlat = `<g transform="translate(${F(hammerX + u * 0.32)} ${F(tTop - u * 0.144)}) rotate(76)">${hm.parts.map(([c, d]) => `<path class="${c}" d="${d}"/>`).join('')}</g>`;. At 76 degrees the claw tip (0.13, 0.07) and the butt (0, 0.6) both land about 0.143u below the pivot. Tune the angle so both touch tTop. Delete hx.

proposals.title: The evening planet sits half under the window frame
proposals.versions: Night (disc half hidden), Dusk and Sunset (halo glowing at the corner); also 1440
proposals.observed: Venus keeps its true offset from the Moon's painted place (about 3.4 to 3.5 degrees left and 1.9 to 2.2 degrees up: 44 to 46 px left and 24 to 28 px up at 1920). With moonAt at 0.38 of the upper pane, it lands at (581.6, 19.7). That is the window's top-left inner corner, where the frame (16.9 to 20.3) hides half its disc. At Dusk (y 15.5) the disc is hidden and only its halo glows at the corner. The pane is too short (37 px) to hold both the Moon (r 13) and Venus 24 px above it.
proposals.proposal: Draw a planet only where it stands clear of the window's bars. Give build() the frame's bars as keep-out boxes, which L.planets already honours. A planet that would be half hidden then goes (as the wall would hide it), and the Moon is untouched. The same hook would guard the prompt desk (see prompt-desk-1).
proposals.why: A bright dot and glow peeking from under a frame bar reads as a stray highlight or a screw head at the corner, not as Venus.
proposals.code: PIECES['tool-wall']: bars: (W, H) => { const f = toolFrame(W, H), t = H * 0.012, tr = f.wT + (f.wB - f.wT) * 0.42, mx = f.wx0 + f.ww / 2; return [[f.wx0, f.wT - t, f.wx1, f.wT + t], [f.wx0, tr - t, f.wx1, tr + t], [mx - t, f.wT, mx + t, f.wB], [f.wx0 - t, f.wT, f.wx0 + t, f.wB], [f.wx1 - t, f.wT, f.wx1 + t, f.wB]]; }. build() line 3345: L.planets(vm, m, P.bars ? P.bars(W, H) : [], cls). hits() already skips within 11 px. Confirm with ?isl-moon= on a date when Venus is up.

proposals.title: The transom cuts the rising Sun in half at Dawn
proposals.versions: Dawn (the Sun); the Moon's new place shows at Sunset, Dusk, Night; the transom in all five
proposals.observed: The Dawn Sun is 2.5 degrees up (32.8 px at 1920), centred at y 76.2 in the right pane. The transom is at 75.3 (±1.3), so the bar runs straight through the middle of the disc. At 1440 it crosses 3 px above the centre. Separately, at Sunset and Dusk Venus (offset from the Moon's place) sits at y 28.1 against the top bar's inner edge (26.5), touching the frame.
proposals.proposal: Raise this window's transom to 0.28 of its height, a top light over the lower panes, so the rising Sun sits whole in the lower pane just above the sea (7 px clear at 1920, 9.6 at 1440). Move the Moon's place up to 0.2 of the pane so it stays whole in the smaller upper pane (at 1920 the disc spans 28 to 54 inside 26.5 to 57). Venus then falls wholly behind the wall above the window instead of on its frame.
proposals.why: The owner's Sun rule: soft, whole, in a clear sky, nothing across it. A bar through the middle is the strongest version of the haze wisp he rejected. The move also clears the planet off the frame.
proposals.code: promptDesk line 1993: wT + (wB - wT) * 0.42 -> * 0.28 (the transom). PIECES['prompt-desk'].moonAt (line 3010): (f.hz - f.wT) * 0.38 -> * 0.2. Moon r = sd 0.2766 × 3 × 1.2 × ppd = 13.1 px at 1920, 10.9 px at 1440. Re-render Dawn and Night at 1920, 1440, 1280, 1120. The adaptive alternative: transom = Math.min(0.42 frac, hz - SKY.a.sun[1] * W / 62 - sunR(W) - 4).

proposals.title: The window's reveal is on the wrong jamb
proposals.observed: The reveal strip is drawn down the window's RIGHT inside edge (wx1). The window is at the left of the picture and the viewer stands to its right, so only its LEFT jamb can be seen. The committee room's left-hand window draws it on the left (windowWall side -1).
proposals.proposal: Move the mitred jamb strip to the window's left edge. Keep the sill strip.
proposals.why: This is the same face-consistency fix as the clock tower and mills, and it matches every later window piece.
proposals.code: promptDesk line 1991: polyD([[wx1, wT], [wx1 - rv, wT + rv], [wx1 - rv, wB], [wx1, wB]]) -> polyD([[wx0, wT], [wx0 + rv, wT + rv], [wx0 + rv, wB], [wx0, wB]]). Or use windowWall(W, H, promptFrame(W, H), 'islpwallg', -1) and drop the duplicate gradient def at line 1972.

proposals.title: The sailing boat's light has no column and the boat no reflection
proposals.versions: all five for the reflection; the column at Dawn, Sunset, Dusk, Night
proposals.observed: The sailboat's masthead light comes on (it is in lights[]), but nothing lies on the water under it. The cay's light beside it has its broken column, and the cay has its mirrored reflection. The white sail and hull have none.
proposals.proposal: Lay a broken column of light under the masthead, as under the cay's light. Add the boat's faint reflection, hull and sail mirrored about its own waterline at 0.15, as the tool wall's boats have.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.3 and 19.4: a column under every light over water, and a reflection for every hull and sail. The lit sail is the brightest thing in the window, so its missing reflection shows.
proposals.code: promptDesk after line 1985: const hull = `M${F(sb - Y(0.03))}...Z`, sail = `M${F(sb)}...Z` (the existing strings); s += dashes(streakList(sb, sy + 1, H, rng(617), 0.04, 0.05), 's-vglow', 1, [0.08, 0.16, 0.3]) + `<g opacity=".15"><g transform="translate(0 ${F(2 * sy)}) scale(1 -1)"><path class="isl-vhull" d="${hull}"/><path class="isl-vsail" d="${sail}"/></g></g>`;. Use its own rng (not r): r feeds the handwriting lengths, the book offsets and the orb's sparks, which would all shift otherwise.

proposals.title: The pen floats above the desk's back edge
proposals.observed: The pen starts at dTop - Y(0.006) and rises Y(0.03), so the whole pen lies above the desk's back edge (dTop), over the wall, a slanted stick in mid-air. Everything else on the desk either stands on the back-edge line or lies in the top band between dTop and dFront.
proposals.proposal: Lay the pen in the desk's top band, which is seen a little from above: near end close to the front edge, far end at the back edge, the same slant read as depth.
proposals.why: The owner catches objects that do not meet the ground. A pen lying across the desk top reads as set down; one above the edge reads as hovering.
proposals.code: promptDesk line 2028: `M${F(nx + nW * 0.66)} ${F(dTop - Y(0.006))}l${F(Y(0.2))} ${F(-Y(0.03))}...` -> `M${F(nx + nW * 0.66)} ${F(dTop + Y(0.026))}l${F(Y(0.2))} ${F(-Y(0.02))}l${F(Y(0.014))} ${F(Y(0.005))}l${F(-Y(0.2))} ${F(Y(0.02))}Z`. This keeps it inside dTop to dFront (0.035H) and clear of the notebook stand's lip (to nx + 0.58nW).

proposals.title: Coffee in the mug, and its shaded side, so it reads by Day
proposals.versions: all five (most needed by Day); the same code in the week calendar
proposals.observed: By Day the mug (#f6f3ee) nearly vanishes against the cream wall (#f1ece2): a pale rectangle with a faint handle. In the week calendar (line 2285) the same mug sits over the calendar's cream page and fades the same way. Its top is a flat line, though the eye is above it (hz 0.45H, mug top about 0.63H), so its opening should show.
proposals.proposal: Give the mug its opening: a rim ellipse in the mug's colour with a dark coffee ellipse inside (isl-lbronze), and a soft shade on the side turned from the light. That is the right third here (the window is at the left) and the left third in the week calendar (the window and sconce are at the right).
proposals.why: The owner's caution in reverse: light on light disappears. A dark oval of coffee makes it a mug at a glance, and the eye-level logic is already set by the desk's visible top.
proposals.code: promptDesk line 2039, after the isl-lmug path: + `<ellipse class="isl-lmug" cx="${F(mx)}" cy="${F(mt)}" rx="${F(mw)}" ry="${F(Y(0.008))}"/><ellipse class="isl-lbronze" cx="${F(mx)}" cy="${F(mt + 0.5)}" rx="${F(mw * 0.8)}" ry="${F(Y(0.0055))}"/><path class="isl-lredsh" d="${rect(mx + mw * 0.35, mt, mw * 0.65, dTop - mt)}"/>`. weekCalendar line 2285: the same with sh for dTop and the shade rect at mx - mw.

proposals.title: The orb's glow laid on the desk beneath it
proposals.versions: all five (the orb keeps its own light by Day); part of the orb's step in the pass (--i:3)
proposals.observed: The orb is the picture's brightest light, with a halo and rings, but it lays no light on anything. Its halo (r = 3 orr) has faded to nothing by the desk top 78 px below. The desk under it and the mug beside it stay unlit.
proposals.proposal: Add a soft pool of the orb's hue on the desk's top band under it, inside the orb's group so it comes on with the orb, last.
proposals.why: DESIGN 19.4: every light is a set (light, halo, pool). A glow on the wood grounds the orb in the room and makes it read as a light rather than a sticker. It stays within the one kind-hue accent, since it is the orb's own light.
proposals.code: promptDesk line 2077, inside <g class="isl-vwin isl-vlast" style="--i:3">, first: `<ellipse cx="${F(ox)}" cy="${F(dTop + Y(0.014))}" rx="${F(orr * 1.6)}" ry="${F(Y(0.016))}" fill="url(#islporbh)" opacity=".7"/>`. The gradient islporbh already exists (line 1974).
